title: One Family Becomes the Nations
summary: Genesis 10 traces the peoples of the known world to Noah’s three sons, placing every nation within one human family under God’s rule.
historicalContext: After the flood the earth was repopulated from the eight people who left the ark, and Genesis 10 maps how that single household grew into the peoples Israel knew. Many of the names surface in Egyptian, Hittite, Assyrian, and Babylonian records of the second and first millennia before Christ: Cimmerians and Medes in the north, Ionian Greeks and Cypriots in the western sea, Egypt and Cush to the south, Babylon and Nineveh in Mesopotamia, the Phoenician coastal cities, the Arameans of Syria, and the incense kingdoms of Arabia. Sidon is named while Tyre is absent, and Israel itself is not yet a nation, details that suit an early origin for the list. The chapter therefore rests on real geography and real peoples. It is ancient ethnography written under inspiration, and it shows a breadth of knowledge about the ancient world that no surviving document from that world can match.
literaryContext: The chapter opens the fourth “generations” section of Genesis and stands between the flood narrative and the tower of Babel. It is a segmented genealogy that moves outward to show how peoples relate, and its order is deliberate: Japheth first, Ham second, and Shem last, so that the chosen line can lead straight into Abram. Three refrains (10:5, 20, 31) close the branches with families, tongues, lands, and nations, and verse 32 answers verse 1 as a frame. Seventy names in all present the nations as a complete whole. Three figures receive pauses in the list: Nimrod, the builder of Babel; Canaan, whose borders are paced out; and Eber, whose son Peleg marks the dividing of the earth. Chapter 10 describes the scattered nations; chapter 11 then tells how the scattering began.
themes: The unity of the human family descended from Noah
God’s blessing of fruitfulness fulfilled after judgment
The rise of cities, kingdoms, and human power
The land of Canaan marked out for later promise
The chosen line preserved through Shem and Eber
The nations held within God’s saving purpose

outline.title: The Generations of Noah’s Sons
outline.summary: The heading introduces the family history of Shem, Ham, and Japheth and the sons born to them after the flood.

outline.title: The Sons of Japheth
outline.summary: Japheth’s seven sons and seven grandsons settle the northern lands and the coastlands of the Mediterranean.

outline.title: Cush, Nimrod, and Mizraim
outline.summary: Ham’s sons are named, Nimrod founds the first kingdom in Shinar and builds into Assyria, and the peoples of Egypt are listed.

outline.title: Canaan and His Borders
outline.summary: Canaan’s eleven descendants are named and the boundaries of the land later promised to Abraham are traced.

outline.title: The Sons of Shem and Eber
outline.summary: Shem’s line runs through Eber, Peleg’s days bring the dividing of the earth, and Joktan’s sons settle Arabia.

outline.title: The Nations Divided After the Flood
outline.summary: A closing summary gathers all the families of Noah’s sons and anticipates their dispersion across the earth.

verses.bibleText: Now these are the generations of the sons of Noah, Shem, Ham, and Japheth: and unto them were sons born after the flood.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“These are the generations” marks a new section of Genesis, the fourth time the formula has appeared (2:4; 5:1; 6:9). Each time it introduces what grew out of the person named. Here the subject is not Noah alone but his three sons, and what grew out of them is the whole range of peoples known to the ancient world. The heading lists them in their familiar order, Shem, Ham, and Japheth, yet the chapter will treat them in reverse, beginning with Japheth and ending with Shem. Genesis often handles the side branches first and saves the chosen line for last, as it does with Cain and Seth, Ishmael and Isaac, Esau and Jacob. Shem’s descendants come last so that the story can move directly from Eber to Abram.

“Unto them were sons born after the flood” ties the chapter to what God said when Noah left the ark: “Be fruitful, and multiply, and replenish the earth” (9:1). The phrasing is passive. Noah’s sons receive their children; life is given to them. After a judgment that swept away every person outside the ark, the earth is filling again because God keeps his word.

The point of greatest weight is that every name in the chapter descends from one household. Only eight people came through the waters (1 Peter 3:20). Nations that would later fight one another, despise one another, or forget one another all share a single origin. Paul made this point at Athens when he declared that God “hath made of one blood all nations of men” (Acts 17:26). No people group stands outside the human family, and none can claim a separate or superior beginning.

The table also prepares for the gospel. Luke traces the genealogy of Jesus back through Shem and Noah to Adam (Luke 3:36-38), so the Saviour belongs to the whole race this chapter describes. The nations listed here are the nations whom Abraham’s Seed will bless.

wordNotes.explanation: Derived from the verb for bearing children, toledot introduces an account of what came from a person: descendants, and often the story of their lives. It is the structural marker of Genesis. Here it introduces a list of peoples rather than a chain of individuals, showing that the term can cover a family history in the widest sense.

wordNotes.term: וַיִּוָּלְדוּ לָהֶם בָּנִים (vayyivvaledu lahem banim) — unto them were sons born
wordNotes.explanation: The passive verb makes Noah’s sons the receivers of offspring. It is the only passive form of “beget” in the chapter, and it frames the multiplying of humanity as the outworking of the blessing God spoke after the flood.

verses.bibleText: The sons of Japheth; Gomer, and Magog, and Madai, and Javan, and Tubal, and Meshech, and Tiras.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Japheth’s seven sons represent peoples on the northern and western edge of Israel’s world, mostly in Anatolia, the lands around the Black Sea, the Iranian highlands, and the Aegean. Gomer corresponds to the people Assyrian records call the Gimirrai, the Cimmerians of Greek writers, horsemen from beyond the Black Sea who pressed into Asia Minor in the eighth and seventh centuries before Christ. Magog is harder to place; it lay somewhere in the far north, and Ezekiel names “Gog, the land of Magog” together with Meshech and Tubal as a coalition gathered against God’s people (Ezekiel 38:2). Revelation takes up Gog and Magog as a picture of the nations marshalled against the beloved city after the thousand years (Revelation 20:8).

Madai is the Medes, who later joined Babylon in destroying Nineveh and then united with Persia, the power that conquered Babylon in Daniel’s day (Daniel 5:28). Javan is the Ionian Greeks of the Aegean coast; in later Hebrew the name stands for Greece as a whole, so that Daniel’s “king of Grecia” is literally the king of Javan (Daniel 8:21). Tubal and Meshech match the Tabal and Mushku of Assyrian texts in eastern and central Anatolia, traders in bronze vessels and slaves in Tyre’s markets (Ezekiel 27:13). Tiras is the least certain, possibly the Tursha, a seafaring people of the Aegean.

The names are both ancestors and peoples, and the list joins the family story of Genesis to nations whose rise and fall would fill the later prophets. Many of these peoples stood far from Israel’s daily life, yet they are counted here as kin.

wordNotes.explanation: Noah’s blessing, “God shall enlarge Japheth,” plays on the sound of the name with the verb yapht, “make wide.” The wide spread of Japheth’s descendants across the north and the western sea shows that word of blessing taking shape in history.

The name corresponds to the Ionians of western Asia Minor. In later books it designates Greece generally, whether as traders in Tyre, buyers of captives from Judah, or the empire of Alexander in Daniel’s visions. Isaiah lists Javan among distant peoples who will hear of God’s glory.

verses.bibleText: And the sons of Gomer; Ashkenaz, and Riphath, and Togarmah.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Gomer’s three sons carry the list further into the north. Ashkenaz is usually linked with the Ashkuza of Assyrian records, a people associated with the Scythians, who appear near Lake Urmia in the seventh century before Christ. Jeremiah summons “the kingdoms of Ararat, Minni, and Ashchenaz” against Babylon (Jeremiah 51:27), placing them in the highlands of Armenia.

Riphath is otherwise unknown; the parallel list in 1 Chronicles 1:6 reads Diphath, since the Hebrew letters for r and d are easily confused. Togarmah corresponds to Tegarama in Hittite and Assyrian texts, in eastern Anatolia. Ezekiel describes “the house of Togarmah” trading horses and mules at Tyre (Ezekiel 27:14) and marching with Gog from “the north quarters” (Ezekiel 38:6).

wordNotes.explanation: In the Old Testament the name refers to a northern people in the region of Ararat. Much later, medieval Jewish writers applied it to the lands of central Europe, which is why Jews of that region came to be called Ashkenazim. That later usage does not determine the meaning in Genesis.

verses.bibleText: And the sons of Javan; Elishah, and Tarshish, Kittim, and Dodanim.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Javan’s four sons are peoples of the Mediterranean islands and coasts. Elishah is most likely Alashiya, the name for Cyprus in second-millennium texts, though Ezekiel’s “isles of Elishah,” a source of blue and purple cloth for Tyre, may point to a wider Greek-speaking region (Ezekiel 27:7). Tarshish was a far western port reached only by sea, rich in silver, iron, tin, and lead (Ezekiel 27:12), probably Tartessus in southern Spain. It was the destination Jonah chose when he fled from the presence of the LORD (Jonah 1:3), and “ships of Tarshish” became a byword for large ocean-going vessels.

Kittim is Kition on the southern coast of Cyprus. Over time the name broadened to describe western sea powers in general (Numbers 24:24; Daniel 11:30). Dodanim appears as Rodanim in 1 Chronicles 1:7 and in the Greek Old Testament, a reading that would point to the island of Rhodes. Taken together, Javan’s line covers the sea lanes from the Aegean to the far west.

wordNotes.explanation: The name may be connected with smelting or refining, which fits a mining region. In the Old Testament Tarshish marks the western edge of the known world: Solomon’s fleets, Tyre’s commerce, and Jonah’s flight all point there, and Isaiah foresees messengers sent to Tarshish to declare God’s glory among the nations.

verses.bibleText: By these were the isles of the Gentiles divided in their lands; every one after his tongue, after their families, in their nations.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“By these were the isles of the Gentiles divided in their lands” closes Japheth’s branch with the first of three refrains (10:20, 31). The “isles” are coastlands, the shores and islands of the Mediterranean that were reached by sea. The verse also signals that the list is selective. The fourteen names of verses 2–4 are heads of larger groupings, and from them many further peoples branched out by the time Genesis was written.

Four terms describe the result: lands, tongues, families, and nations. Territory, language, kinship, and political identity all mark human life after the flood. The mention of separate tongues comes before the account of Babel, which explains how languages were confused (11:7-9). Genesis arranges the material by topic: chapter 10 describes the scattered world, and chapter 11 goes back to tell how the scattering began.

The verb “divided” anticipates verse 32 and echoes Moses’ song: “When the most High divided to the nations their inheritance, when he separated the sons of Adam, he set the bounds of the people” (Deuteronomy 32:8). The spread of peoples was not random. God assigned their places. Paul says the same at Athens and gives the reason: that they “should seek the Lord, if haply they might feel after him, and find him” (Acts 17:27).

The coastlands, the most distant region on Israel’s horizon, receive repeated promises in the prophets. Isaiah says that “the isles shall wait for his law” when the Servant brings justice to the earth (Isaiah 42:4), and that survivors will be sent to Tarshish, Tubal, Javan, and “the isles afar off” to declare God’s glory (Isaiah 66:19). The apostles later carried the gospel through the lands of Javan, and the gospel reached Europe from there. Peoples who seemed farthest from the covenant were never outside God’s concern.

wordNotes.term: אִיֵּי הַגּוֹיִם (iyye haggoyim) — isles of the Gentiles
wordNotes.explanation: The word iyyim covers islands and coastlands alike, the lands one reaches by sailing. In the prophets the term often stands for the farthest nations, which will hear of God’s salvation. The KJV’s “Gentiles” translates goyim, the ordinary word for nations.

Throughout the chapter the peoples are called goyim, nations defined by territory and government. The more intimate word ʿam, “people,” often used of Israel as the LORD’s people, never appears in the table. The vocabulary describes the nations as political communities and leaves Israel’s covenant identity for later chapters.

verses.bibleText: And the sons of Ham; Cush, and Mizraim, and Phut, and Canaan.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The second branch turns south and toward the lands Israel knew best. Cush is the region beyond Egypt’s southern frontier along the upper Nile, later called Nubia and, in the KJV, Ethiopia. Mizraim is Egypt itself, the land where Israel would first find refuge and then bondage; the psalmist even calls it “the land of Ham” (Psalm 105:23). Put is generally placed in Africa as well. The Greek Old Testament renders it “Libya,” though some connect it with Punt, the coastland on the Red Sea that Egyptian expeditions visited for incense and ebony. Canaan, already named in 9:18–25, is the coastal and hill country between Egypt and Syria.

The grouping reflects history and geography more than language. Canaanites spoke a Semitic tongue closely related to Hebrew, yet they stand under Ham, while later in the chapter Elam, whose language was not Semitic, appears under Shem. The table describes how peoples were connected in the ancient world, and it should not be read as a modern classification by race or speech.

This matters because Noah’s curse fell on Canaan alone (9:25), not on Ham’s other sons, and never on any skin color. Scripture honors Cushites repeatedly. Moses married a Cushite woman and God rebuked those who criticized him for it (Numbers 12:1-10). Ebed-melech the Ethiopian rescued Jeremiah from the pit and received God’s promise of deliverance (Jeremiah 38:7-13; 39:16-18). The psalmist foresaw that “Ethiopia shall soon stretch out her hands unto God” (Psalm 68:31), and an Ethiopian official was among the first Gentiles baptized into Christ (Acts 8:27-38).

wordNotes.explanation: This is the regular Hebrew name for Egypt. Its ending looks like a dual, which may reflect the ancient division into Upper and Lower Egypt, the “Two Lands” of Egyptian royal titles. The name survives in the Arabic Misr. In Genesis the word is both a son of Ham and the country his descendants occupied.

Cush usually names the Nile kingdom south of Egypt. Its people were known for stature and military strength, and in the eighth century before Christ Cushite kings ruled Egypt itself. Some of Cush’s sons in the next verse settled across the Red Sea in Arabia, so the name could extend to related peoples there.

verses.bibleText: And the sons of Cush; Seba, and Havilah, and Sabtah, and Raamah, and Sabtecha: and the sons of Raamah; Sheba, and Dedan.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Cush’s five sons and two grandsons belong mainly to the shores of the Red Sea and the southern half of Arabia. Seba is connected with Africa in Isaiah, who names it beside Egypt and Cush and describes its people as “men of stature” (Isaiah 43:3; 45:14). Havilah lay in Arabia, at the edge of the wilderness where Ishmael’s descendants later lived (25:18; 1 Samuel 15:7). Sabtah may correspond to Shabwa, the ancient capital of Hadramaut, while Sabtecha remains unidentified. Raamah was a trading people of southwest Arabia who brought spices, precious stones, and gold to the markets of Tyre (Ezekiel 27:22).

Raamah’s sons are better known. Sheba became the wealthy kingdom of the Sabaeans in what is now Yemen, famous for incense and for the queen who visited Solomon (1 Kings 10:1-10). Dedan was a merchant people of northern Arabia (Ezekiel 27:20). Sheba and Havilah appear again in Joktan’s line (vv. 28–29), and Sheba and Dedan among Abraham’s descendants through Keturah (25:3). Trade, migration, and intermarriage brought these Arabian peoples into more than one family relationship.

These far southern lands appear in Israel’s hope for the nations. “The kings of Sheba and Seba shall offer gifts” to the righteous King (Psalm 72:10), and those from Sheba will come bearing gold and incense to “shew forth the praises of the LORD” (Isaiah 60:6). The wise men who brought gold, frankincense, and myrrh to the child Jesus enacted that hope in part (Matthew 2:11).

wordNotes.term: שְׁבָא (Sheva) and סְבָא (Seva) — Sheba and Seba
wordNotes.explanation: The two names differ only in their first letter, shin and samekh. Seba is linked with Africa and Cush; Sheba is the Arabian kingdom of the Sabaeans. Psalm 72 names both together to describe the farthest southern kings bowing before the Messiah.

verses.bibleText: And Cush begat Nimrod: he began to be a mighty one in the earth.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The list suddenly pauses. Instead of another name with the formula “the sons of,” Genesis says that “Cush begat Nimrod” and then gives a brief biography, the longest comment on any individual in the chapter. Nimrod is a person, not a people, and what he did matters more to the writer than where his descendants lived.

“He began to be a mighty one in the earth.” The verb “began” often marks a new development in Genesis: people began to call on the name of the LORD (4:26), men began to multiply (6:1), Noah began to be a husbandman (9:20). With Nimrod something new appears after the flood, the rise of one man to dominance over others. He is the first figure in Scripture said to have a kingdom (10:10). The title “mighty one” echoes the “mighty men which were of old, men of renown” before the flood (6:4), in an age the earth was filled with violence. The same impulse that brought judgment then reappears within a few generations of Noah.

That a son of Cush founds cities in Mesopotamia is unexpected, but Scripture consistently ties Nimrod to that region; Micah calls Assyria “the land of Nimrod” (Micah 5:6). His name sounds like the Hebrew for “we will rebel,” and Jewish tradition long remembered him as the leader of the rebellion at Babel. Genesis does not spell this out, but placing him beside Babel in the next verses invites the connection.

Nimrod stands as the first portrait of power built by human force. Jesus set a different pattern before his disciples: the rulers of the Gentiles lord it over others, “but it shall not be so among you,” for the Son of man came “not to be ministered unto, but to minister” (Matthew 20:25-28). Christ’s kingdom grows by service and self-giving, the reverse of Nimrod’s method.

wordNotes.explanation: The word describes a strong warrior or champion. It can be used positively, as of David’s mighty men or of God himself as a mighty warrior, but here it recalls the violent heroes of Genesis 6:4. Context shows a man whose strength made him a ruler over others.

The name resembles a Hebrew verb form meaning “we will rebel,” from marad, “to rebel.” Whether or not this was its original meaning, the sound fits the role Genesis gives him as the founder of Babel and of the Mesopotamian kingdoms. No surviving ancient record names him directly.

verses.bibleText: He was a mighty hunter before the LORD: wherefore it is said, Even as Nimrod the mighty hunter before the LORD.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“He was a mighty hunter before the LORD: wherefore it is said, Even as Nimrod the mighty hunter before the LORD.” Nimrod’s fame was such that his name became a proverb, a standard of comparison for any outstanding hunter or warrior. Kings in the ancient Near East prized the hunt as a display of royal strength. Assyrian palace reliefs show rulers killing lions from chariots, and their inscriptions boast of beasts slain alongside cities conquered. Hunting and war belonged together in the image of kingship.

The phrase “before the LORD” is open to more than one sense. It can mean that Nimrod’s prowess was remarkable even in God’s sight, a way of saying he was the greatest hunter of his time. The Greek Old Testament uses a preposition that can mean either “before” or “against,” and from early times many readers took the phrase as opposition: Nimrod made his name in defiance of the LORD. The context leans that way. His greatness is tied to the founding of Babel, and the next chapter shows Babel’s builders seeking a name for themselves apart from God (11:4).

Either way, nothing Nimrod did was hidden from God. His strength was exercised “before the LORD,” under the eye of the One who “sitteth in the heavens” and laughs at the plans of rulers set against him (Psalm 2:2-4). Genesis is also wary of the hunter as a type. Esau, “a cunning hunter, a man of the field,” sold his birthright, while the promise passed to Jacob (25:27-34).

The proverb preserves Nimrod’s name, but the name God values is of another kind. To Abram, who would build altars, God said, “I will make thy name great” (12:2). A name received from God through faith outlasts any name won by conquest.

wordNotes.explanation: Tsayid is the ordinary word for game or hunting. Combined with gibbor it describes a champion of the chase. In royal ideology of the ancient Near East, the hunter-king protected his realm from wild beasts and displayed the same force he used against enemies, so the title suggests both hunting and conquest.

wordNotes.term: לִפְנֵי יְהוָה (lifne YHWH) — before the LORD
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “to the face of the LORD,” the phrase usually means in God’s presence or sight. It can carry a superlative sense, “exceedingly great,” as when Nineveh is called “great to God.” The Greek translation’s enantion can also mean “against,” which gave rise to the long-standing reading of Nimrod as an opponent of God.

verses.bibleText: And the beginning of his kingdom was Babel, and Erech, and Accad, and Calneh, in the land of Shinar.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“The beginning of his kingdom was Babel, and Erech, and Accad, and Calneh, in the land of Shinar.” This is the first use of the word “kingdom” in the Bible, and it is tied from the start to Babel. The word translated “beginning” can mean either the first stage of Nimrod’s realm or its chief cities, and both are true. Southern Mesopotamia was the base from which his power spread.

Babel is Babylon on the Euphrates, later the capital of Hammurabi and, centuries afterward, of Nebuchadnezzar, who destroyed Jerusalem. Erech is Uruk, modern Warka, one of the oldest and largest cities of Sumer; men from Erech were among those the Assyrians later settled in Samaria (Ezra 4:9). Accad is Agade, the seat of Sargon’s dynasty, whose ruins have never been found but whose name passed to the Akkadian language. Calneh is uncertain. It may be Nippur, an important religious center, or the consonants may be read as “all of them,” so that the verse means “Babel, Erech, and Accad, all of them in the land of Shinar.”

Shinar is the biblical name for Babylonia. It is where Babel’s builders settle (11:2), where Nebuchadnezzar carries the vessels of God’s house into the treasure house of his god (Daniel 1:2), and where Zechariah sees wickedness carried in an ephah to have a house built for it (Zechariah 5:11). From its first mention the land is linked to human pride and false worship.

This gives the verse weight far beyond geography. Babylon becomes Scripture’s great symbol of organized resistance to God. In Revelation it stands for the end-time union of religious and political power that leads the world into false worship, and God’s final call to his people is, “Come out of her, my people, that ye be not partakers of her sins” (Revelation 18:4). The story of Babylon begins here with Nimrod and ends with its fall at the coming of Christ (Revelation 14:8; 18:2). Between the two stands the city whose builder and maker is God (Hebrews 11:10).

wordNotes.term: רֵאשִׁית מַמְלַכְתּוֹ (reshit mamlakhto) — the beginning of his kingdom
wordNotes.explanation: Reshit, the same word that opens Genesis, means first in time or first in rank. Mamlakah, “kingdom,” appears here for the first time in Scripture. The phrase presents the cities of Shinar as the original and principal centers of Nimrod’s rule.

Shinar designates the whole of Babylonia, the alluvial plain of the lower Tigris and Euphrates. The biblical writers use the name with consistent associations of empire and idolatry, from the tower of Babel to the exile and the prophets’ visions.

verses.bibleText: Out of that land went forth Asshur, and builded Nineveh, and the city Rehoboth, and Calah,

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Out of that land went forth Asshur, and builded Nineveh.” The KJV takes Asshur as the subject, which could refer to Shem’s son of that name (10:22). The Hebrew can just as easily be read with Nimrod still the subject: “Out of that land he went forth into Assyria.” Since Micah calls Assyria “the land of Nimrod” (Micah 5:6), the second reading fits well. In either case the movement is from Babylonia northward up the Tigris, and the power that began in Shinar extends into Assyria.

Nineveh lay on the east bank of the Tigris, opposite modern Mosul. It grew into the capital of the Assyrian Empire, whose armies destroyed Samaria and the northern kingdom of Israel and besieged Jerusalem in Hezekiah’s day. Rehoboth-Ir means “broad places of the city” and may refer to the open quarters or suburbs of Nineveh. Calah is Kalhu, modern Nimrud, about twenty miles south of Nineveh, where the Tigris meets the Upper Zab. It served as Assyria’s capital in the ninth century before Christ, and its ruins yielded the Black Obelisk of Shalmaneser III, which shows Jehu king of Israel bowing with tribute.

Nineveh’s later history shows God’s mercy reaching even the cities of Nimrod. When Jonah preached, the city repented, and God spared it, asking whether he should not pity “that great city” with its many people and cattle (Jonah 4:11). Jesus pointed to that repentance as a rebuke to his own generation (Matthew 12:41).

wordNotes.explanation: The word names a person, the god of the Assyrians, their oldest capital city, and the nation as a whole. Hebrew syntax allows it to be either the subject of “went forth” or the destination, “to Assyria.” The second reading is supported by Micah’s phrase “the land of Nimrod.”

Nineveh was the most famous city of Assyria and its capital at the height of its power. The prophets denounced its cruelty, and Nahum announced its fall, which came in 612 before Christ, yet Jonah records its repentance and God’s compassion toward it.

verses.bibleText: And Resen between Nineveh and Calah: the same is a great city.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Resen is placed “between Nineveh and Calah,” but its site has not been identified. It may have been a smaller town or part of the urban complex that grew up between the two great cities.

“The same is a great city” could describe Calah, the last city named, or the entire cluster of Nineveh, Rehoboth-Ir, Calah, and Resen viewed as one. The book of Jonah calls Nineveh “that great city” and “an exceeding great city of three days’ journey” (Jonah 1:2; 3:3), a description that may reflect such a wider metropolitan region. Genesis here introduces Nineveh as the second great center of human power after Babylon.

Nimrod’s legacy is a landscape of cities. Abraham, by contrast, will dwell in tents and build altars, because “he looked for a city which hath foundations, whose builder and maker is God” (Hebrews 11:10).

wordNotes.term: הָעִיר הַגְּדֹלָה (ha'ir haggedolah) — the great city
wordNotes.explanation: The phrase recurs in Jonah for Nineveh and in Revelation, in its Greek form, for Babylon. It marks a city as a center of power and population. Here it may cover the whole complex of Assyrian cities just listed.

verses.bibleText: And Mizraim begat Ludim, and Anamim, and Lehabim, and Naphtuhim,

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Mizraim’s descendants are listed with the plural ending -im, which marks them as peoples rather than single ancestors. Their homes lay in Egypt and along its borders. The Ludim, distinct from Shem’s son Lud (10:22), appear in the prophets with Cush and Put as soldiers who “handle and bend the bow” in Egypt’s armies (Jeremiah 46:9; Ezekiel 30:5), which suggests a North African people. The Anamim are unidentified, though an Assyrian text mentions a people of similar name in the region of Cyrene.

The Lehabim are probably the Libyans west of the Nile Delta, called Lubim elsewhere, who fought alongside Egypt (2 Chronicles 12:3; Nahum 3:9). The Naphtuhim may be “the people of Ptah,” the god of Memphis, and so the inhabitants of Lower Egypt. Together these names sketch the regions and border peoples that made up Egypt’s world.

wordNotes.explanation: The name likely corresponds to the Lebu of Egyptian inscriptions, Libyan tribes northwest of Egypt who repeatedly pressed on its frontier. In later books the related form Lubim describes Libyan troops serving with Egyptian and Cushite forces.

verses.bibleText: And Pathrusim, and Casluhim, (out of whom came Philistim,) and Caphtorim.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The Pathrusim are the people of Pathros, an Egyptian name meaning “the southland,” that is, Upper Egypt. Ezekiel calls Pathros “the land of their habitation,” the original home of the Egyptians (Ezekiel 29:14), and after the fall of Jerusalem some Jews took refuge there (Jeremiah 44:1). The Casluhim have not been identified.

The parenthesis “out of whom came Philistim” introduces the people who would become Israel’s persistent rivals on the southern coast. Amos and Jeremiah trace the Philistines to Caphtor (Amos 9:7; Jeremiah 47:4), so the note may belong with the Caphtorim, or Philistine groups may have arisen from both related peoples. Caphtor is generally identified with Crete, the Keftiu of Egyptian texts, from which seafaring peoples spread around the eastern Mediterranean. The Caphtorim drove out earlier inhabitants of the coast as far as Gaza (Deuteronomy 2:23). The later name Palestine comes from the Philistines.

Amos uses this history to make a striking point. The LORD who brought Israel out of Egypt also brought “the Philistines from Caphtor, and the Syrians from Kir” (Amos 9:7). The movements of every nation are under his direction, and Israel’s election never made other peoples insignificant to God. The psalmist even foresees Philistia among those of whom it will be said, “this man was born there,” in Zion (Psalm 87:4).

wordNotes.explanation: The Philistines appear in Egyptian records as one of the Sea Peoples who settled the southern coastal plain of Canaan. Their five cities included Gaza, Ashdod, and Ashkelon. The word gave rise to the Greek Palaistinē and the later name Palestine.

Caphtor corresponds to Kaptara in Mesopotamian texts and Keftiu in Egyptian ones, names for Crete and the Aegean world connected with it. Jeremiah calls it “the country of Caphtor” and an isle, consistent with an island setting.

verses.bibleText: And Canaan begat Sidon his firstborn, and Heth,

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Canaan’s line is introduced with the same verb used for Cush and Mizraim, “begat,” and it receives eleven names, more than any other descendant of Ham. The attention reflects the land’s importance in the coming story. These are the peoples whose territory God will give to Abraham’s seed (12:7; 15:18-21).

Sidon, Canaan’s firstborn, was the leading Phoenician port on the coast of what is now Lebanon. Joshua knew it as “great Zidon” (Joshua 11:8), and its people were so prominent that “Sidonians” could describe Phoenicians in general. Tyre, which later overshadowed Sidon, is not mentioned at all, a detail that fits an early date for the list. The Phoenician seafarers later spread their trade and colonies across the Mediterranean.

Heth is the ancestor of the “sons of Heth” or Hittites who lived around Hebron in Abraham’s day. From them Abraham bought the cave of Machpelah to bury Sarah, carefully paying full price (23:3-20). Esau’s Hittite wives were “a grief of mind” to Isaac and Rebekah (26:34-35; 27:46). Whether these Hittites of Canaan were linked to the great Hittite empire of Anatolia is uncertain; the biblical Hittites bear Semitic names and live among the Canaanite peoples.

Centuries later Jesus went into the region of Tyre and Sidon, where a woman of Canaan begged him to heal her daughter. He commended her faith and granted her request (Matthew 15:21-28). Noah’s word about Canaan (9:25) did not shut any Canaanite out from the mercy of God.

wordNotes.term: צִידֹן בְּכֹרוֹ (Tsidon bekhoro) — Sidon his firstborn
wordNotes.explanation: Bekhor, “firstborn,” gives Sidon priority among Canaan’s descendants, matching the city’s early leadership among the Phoenician coastal states. The tribe of Asher was later unable to drive out its inhabitants.

The name stands behind the expressions “sons of Heth” and “Hittites.” In Genesis these people are settled residents of Hebron who deal courteously with Abraham, and Ezekiel later describes Jerusalem’s origins as Amorite and Hittite to expose its pagan character.

verses.bibleText: And the Jebusite, and the Amorite, and the Girgasite,

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The list shifts from personal names to peoples, using the form that means “the one of” a clan: the Jebusite, the Amorite, the Girgasite. The Jebusites held Jerusalem, then called Jebus, until David captured the stronghold of Zion (2 Samuel 5:6-9). Araunah the Jebusite sold David the threshing floor on which the temple was later built (2 Samuel 24:18-24; 2 Chronicles 3:1), so a Canaanite plot became the place of Israel’s sacrifices.

The Amorites were widely spread; Mesopotamian texts used the name for peoples of the west. In Canaan they lived in the hill country on both sides of the Jordan (Numbers 13:29). God told Abraham that the land would not be given to his descendants until “the iniquity of the Amorites” was full (15:16), revealing divine patience over centuries. The Girgasites are known only from the biblical lists of Canaan’s inhabitants (Joshua 24:11).

wordNotes.explanation: The name sometimes stands for the inhabitants of Canaan as a whole, especially in the hill country. Amos recalls the Amorite as tall like cedars and strong as oaks, yet destroyed before Israel. God’s timing for that judgment shows that he waited until their wickedness had run its course.

verses.bibleText: And the Hivite, and the Arkite, and the Sinite,

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The Hivites lived at Shechem in Jacob’s day (34:2), at Gibeon in Joshua’s day, where they secured peace with Israel by a ruse (Joshua 9:3-7), and in the region of Hermon and Lebanon (Joshua 11:3; Judges 3:3). The Gibeonites later served at the house of God, a remarkable outcome for a people under the ban.

The Arkites and Sinites belong to the northern Phoenician coast. Arka, known in ancient texts as Irqata, lay in the foothills north of modern Tripoli. The Sinites are linked with Siyannu, a small city-state near Ugarit. Neither people figures in the conquest narratives, which focus on the land further south.

wordNotes.explanation: The Hivites are known mainly from Scripture. Their towns at Shechem and Gibeon show them living in central Canaan, and a group of them in the north near Hermon. Some connect them with the Horites, since the Greek translation occasionally interchanges the two names.

verses.bibleText: And the Arvadite, and the Zemarite, and the Hamathite: and afterward were the families of the Canaanites spread abroad.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Three more northern peoples complete the list. The Arvadites inhabited Arvad, an island city off the northern Phoenician coast, whose men served Tyre as oarsmen and soldiers (Ezekiel 27:8, 11). The Zemarites belonged to Sumur, a coastal town south of Arvad that appears in Egyptian and Amarna records. The Hamathites lived at Hamath on the Orontes River in Syria. “The entering in of Hamath” later served as the northern limit of the land promised to Israel (Numbers 34:8; 1 Kings 8:65).

“And afterward were the families of the Canaanites spread abroad.” The verb anticipates chapter 11, where the same root describes the builders’ fear of being “scattered abroad” and God’s act of scattering them (11:4, 8-9). Canaan’s clans spread through the land until they filled it from the coast to the Jordan valley, setting the stage for the next verse.

wordNotes.explanation: The verb puts means to scatter or disperse. In Genesis it links the spreading of the nations to the judgment at Babel, and later prophets use it for the scattering of Israel in exile and for God’s promise to gather the dispersed again.

verses.bibleText: And the border of the Canaanites was from Sidon, as thou comest to Gerar, unto Gaza; as thou goest, unto Sodom, and Gomorrah, and Admah, and Zeboim, even unto Lasha.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Only two families in the table receive borders: Canaan here and Joktan in verse 30. The detail given to Canaan is purposeful, because this is the land God will promise to Abraham and his seed (12:7; 15:18). Moses records its limits long before Israel enters it, much as Numbers later sets out its full boundaries before the conquest (Numbers 34:2-12).

The description moves along two lines. The first runs south along the coast “from Sidon, as thou comest to Gerar, unto Gaza.” Gerar, near Gaza, is where Abraham and Isaac later sojourned with Abimelech (20:1; 26:1). Gaza became one of the Philistine cities. The second line turns inland toward “Sodom, and Gomorrah, and Admah, and Zeboim, even unto Lasha,” the cities of the plain near the Dead Sea. Lasha’s location is unknown, though it must have lain in the same region.

The four cities of the plain are named here as living places. Readers who know the coming story feel the weight of the list, for all four will be overthrown when the LORD rains fire and brimstone on them (19:24-25; Deuteronomy 29:23). Hosea uses Admah and Zeboim as a byword for complete destruction, and then hears God say, “How shall I give thee up, Ephraim?” (Hosea 11:8). Judgment on these cities came only after their wickedness was full and after Abraham’s intercession had been heard (18:23-33).

The land belongs to the LORD, who gives it as he wills (Leviticus 25:23). The promise to Abraham reaches beyond Canaan’s borders as well, for Paul calls him “the heir of the world” through the righteousness of faith (Romans 4:13), and Jesus promises that the meek “shall inherit the earth” (Matthew 5:5).

wordNotes.explanation: The word means a boundary line and, by extension, the territory it encloses. Its use here anticipates the boundaries God fixes for Israel and the nations, and the law forbade moving a neighbor’s landmark because borders were held as a trust from God.

wordNotes.term: אַדְמָה וּצְבֹיִם (Admah uTsevoyim) — Admah and Zeboim
wordNotes.explanation: These two cities are always named with Sodom and Gomorrah or with each other. Their kings fought in the war of chapter 14, and their overthrow made them proverbial for total judgment, yet Hosea uses the same names to reveal God’s reluctance to destroy his people.

verses.bibleText: These are the sons of Ham, after their families, after their tongues, in their countries, and in their nations.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Ham’s branch closes with its refrain: “after their families, after their tongues, in their countries, and in their nations.” The four terms match those of verse 5, though here they begin with families and end with nations, an order that verse 31 will repeat.

Ham’s descendants include the powers that most shaped Israel’s history: Egypt, which enslaved them; Babylon and Assyria, which carried them into exile; the Canaanites, among whom they lived; and the Philistines, who fought them for generations. Yet the refrain treats these nations exactly as it treats the others. Each has its families, language, and land within the order God set after the flood.

Isaiah later announces a future that would have astonished an Israelite reader. “In that day shall Israel be the third with Egypt and with Assyria, even a blessing in the midst of the land: whom the LORD of hosts shall bless, saying, Blessed be Egypt my people, and Assyria the work of my hands, and Israel mine inheritance” (Isaiah 19:24-25). The nations of Ham’s line, including Israel’s oppressors, are among those God intends to bring into his family.

wordNotes.explanation: A mishpachah is a clan, a kinship group larger than a household and smaller than a tribe or nation. The word reappears in God’s promise to Abram that “in thee shall all families of the earth be blessed,” tying the clans of Genesis 10 to the scope of that blessing.

verses.bibleText: Unto Shem also, the father of all the children of Eber, the brother of Japheth the elder, even to him were children born.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The final branch is the one the chapter has been moving toward. “Unto Shem also … even to him were children born.” Shem was named first in verse 1, and his line now comes last, where it can lead without interruption into the genealogy of 11:10-26 and the call of Abram. The arrangement shows where the story is heading.

Before naming a single son, the verse calls Shem “the father of all the children of Eber.” Eber was Shem’s great-grandson (10:24), so this is a deliberate pointer. The word “Hebrew,” ʿIvri, is the family name derived from Eber, and Abram will be the first person called “the Hebrew” (14:13). Yet Eber’s children were more than Israel. Through Joktan they include the Arabian tribes of verses 26–30, and through Peleg the families of Terah, Nahor, Lot, Ishmael, and Esau. The Hebrews belong to a wider kinship that Israel was meant to remember.

“The brother of Japheth the elder” can be read two ways in Hebrew, either making Japheth the elder brother or making Shem the elder brother of Japheth. The KJV’s reading fits the chronology best. Noah began having sons at five hundred (5:32), and Shem was a hundred years old two years after the flood (11:10), when Noah was six hundred and two, so Shem was not the firstborn. He heads the lists because of what God would do through him.

This pattern runs through Genesis and beyond. Abel is accepted over Cain, Isaac is chosen over Ishmael, Jacob over Esau, Judah and Joseph over Reuben, Ephraim over Manasseh. God’s purpose does not depend on the rights of birth order. Shem’s name means “name,” and the blessing Noah pronounced on him (“Blessed be the LORD God of Shem,” 9:26) gave him his significance. Babel’s builders will try to make a name for themselves (11:4); Shem’s line receives its name from God and leads at last to the One whose name is above every name (Philippians 2:9).

wordNotes.explanation: The name is connected with the root for crossing over or the region beyond, and the gentilic ʿIvri, “Hebrew,” is formed from it. Outsiders typically use “Hebrew” for Abraham’s descendants, as Potiphar’s wife and Jonah’s shipmates do. Genesis traces the term to an ancestor whose line is wider than Israel.

wordNotes.term: אֲחִי יֶפֶת הַגָּדוֹל (achi Yefet haggadol) — the brother of Japheth the elder
wordNotes.explanation: The adjective haggadol, “the great” or “the elder,” could modify either Japheth or the word “brother.” The KJV attaches it to Japheth. The ages given in Genesis 5:32 and 11:10 support that reading, showing that Shem’s priority in the lists rests on God’s choice and not on seniority.

verses.bibleText: The children of Shem; Elam, and Asshur, and Arphaxad, and Lud, and Aram.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Shem’s five sons occupy a band of territory from the Iranian highlands across Mesopotamia into Syria and Asia Minor. Elam lay east of the lower Tigris in what is now southwest Iran. Its capital, Susa, the Shushan of Scripture, later became a royal city of Persia, where Daniel saw his vision by the river Ulai and where Esther became queen (Daniel 8:2; Esther 1:2). The Elamites spoke a language unrelated to Hebrew, another reminder that the table groups peoples by descent and history and not by speech.

Asshur is the ancestor whose name passed to Assyria, already mentioned in verse 11 as the region Nimrod’s power reached. Arphaxad is the son through whom the line of promise runs (11:12); his name has not been linked securely with any place. Lud is often connected with the Lydians of western Asia Minor, whose capital Sardis later received one of the letters of Revelation (Revelation 3:1). Aram is the father of the Arameans of Syria and upper Mesopotamia.

The Arameans stand closest to Abraham’s own story. His relatives settled at Haran, Rebekah was “the daughter of Bethuel the Syrian” (25:20), and Israel would confess at the harvest festival, “A Syrian ready to perish was my father” (Deuteronomy 26:5). The Aramaic language later spread across the Near East, appears in parts of Daniel and Ezra, and was spoken by Jesus, whose words “Talitha cumi” Mark preserves (Mark 5:41).

Several of Shem’s peoples reappear at Pentecost, when “Parthians, and Medes, and Elamites, and the dwellers in Mesopotamia” heard the apostles speak in their own tongues “the wonderful works of God” (Acts 2:9-11).

wordNotes.explanation: Aram names both the ancestor and the Aramean peoples, rendered “Syria” and “Syrian” in the KJV. Their territory stretched from Damascus to the Euphrates. Laban the Aramean was Jacob’s uncle, and Aramaic became the common language of the Persian Empire and of Palestine in Jesus’ day.

Elam was an ancient kingdom east of Babylonia. Its king Chedorlaomer led the eastern coalition against the cities of the plain in Abraham’s day, Jeremiah announced both its judgment and its restoration, and Elamites were present in Jerusalem at Pentecost.

verses.bibleText: And the children of Aram; Uz, and Hul, and Gether, and Mash.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Aram’s four sons are given without further descendants. Uz is the most familiar name because Job lived “in the land of Uz” (Job 1:1). The name also belongs to a son of Abraham’s brother Nahor (22:21, “Huz”) and to a Horite descendant of Seir (36:28), and Lamentations links Uz with Edom (Lamentations 4:21), so the region cannot be fixed with certainty.

Hul and Gether are unknown. Mash may be connected with Mount Masius in northern Mesopotamia or with the Lebanon ranges; the parallel in 1 Chronicles 1:17 reads Meshech. These Aramean clans lived in the regions from which Abraham’s family later came.

wordNotes.explanation: Uz is both a personal name and a territory. Because the name occurs in Aramean, Nahorite, and Edomite settings, Job’s homeland is best located generally east of Canaan on the edge of the desert, among peoples with family ties to Abraham.

verses.bibleText: And Arphaxad begat Salah; and Salah begat Eber.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Arphaxad begat Salah; and Salah begat Eber.” Here the wide genealogy narrows for a moment into a single line, the line that chapter 11 will trace with ages and years (11:12-16). Of Shem’s five sons, only Arphaxad’s descendants are followed beyond one generation, because his line leads to Eber and through Eber to Abram.

The Greek Old Testament inserts a Cainan between Arphaxad and Salah, both here and in chapter 11, and the name appears in Luke’s genealogy of Jesus (Luke 3:35-36). The Hebrew text of Genesis and the lists in 1 Chronicles 1:18 and 1:24 have no Cainan. The question concerns the history of the text and does not affect the point of either genealogy: the Messiah descends through Shem and Eber, as God had promised.

Salah’s name may mean “sprout” or “shoot,” an apt word for a branch through which the family of promise continues to grow. Eber, his son, will now become the turning point of the whole Shemite list.

wordNotes.explanation: The name is related to a root meaning to send out, and as a noun it can refer to a shoot or offshoot. Nothing further is recorded of him, but his place in the chain makes him an ancestor of Abraham and of Christ.

verses.bibleText: And unto Eber were born two sons: the name of one was Peleg; for in his days was the earth divided; and his brother's name was Joktan.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And unto Eber were born two sons: the name of one was Peleg; for in his days was the earth divided; and his brother’s name was Joktan.” Apart from Nimrod, Peleg is the only person in the chapter who receives an explanatory comment, and the two comments belong together. Nimrod founded Babel; in Peleg’s days the earth was divided.

The name Peleg means “division.” The verb used for the dividing of the earth, palag, occurs in David’s prayer, “Destroy, O Lord, and divide their tongues” (Psalm 55:9), where it describes confusing human speech. That connection points to the event of the next chapter, when “the LORD did there confound the language of all the earth” and scattered the people (11:9). “The earth” here means its inhabitants, as in 11:1, where “the whole earth was of one language.” The division is of humanity into separate language groups and nations.

Some have proposed that the verse describes the breaking apart of the continents. The text gives no support to that reading. Its concern is people, not landmasses, and the great geological upheavals of Scripture belong to the flood, when “all the fountains of the great deep” were broken up (7:11). Peleg was born, by the ages given in chapter 11, about a century after the flood (11:10-16), so the confusion at Babel took place within a few generations of Noah, while the memory of the flood was still fresh and Noah himself was alive.

Eber’s two sons divide the Shemite line. Joktan’s descendants are listed immediately (10:26-29) and then leave the story. Peleg’s line is held back until 11:16-26, where it leads to Abram. The division of the nations and the setting apart of the line of promise happen side by side.

The New Testament shows God answering Babel’s division. At Pentecost, people “out of every nation under heaven” heard the gospel “every man in our own language” (Acts 2:5-8). Christ “hath broken down the middle wall of partition” between peoples (Ephesians 2:14), and John sees a multitude “of all nations, and kindreds, and people, and tongues” before the throne (Revelation 7:9).

wordNotes.term: פֶּלֶג … נִפְלְגָה (Peleg … niflegah) — Peleg … was divided
wordNotes.explanation: The name and the verb share the root palag, “to divide” or “split.” As a noun peleg can mean a channel or stream of water, a division cut through land. The wordplay explains the name by the events of his lifetime, much as Noah’s name was explained by his father’s hope.

Joktan, Peleg’s brother, is the ancestor of thirteen Arabian peoples. His line is listed in full in the table of nations, while Peleg’s is reserved for the chosen line in chapter 11. Joktan’s descendants are close kin of the Hebrews through Eber.

verses.bibleText: And Joktan begat Almodad, and Sheleph, and Hazarmaveth, and Jerah,

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Joktan’s thirteen sons are the largest single family in the table, and most of the identifiable names belong to southern Arabia. Almodad has not been located. Sheleph corresponds to a Yemeni tribe whose name survives in local place names. Hazarmaveth is Hadramaut, the region along the south coast of Arabia known for frankincense and myrrh. Jerah, a word meaning “moon,” remains unidentified.

These Semitic peoples of Arabia stand alongside the Cushite Arabians of verse 7 and the later Arab descendants of Abraham through Ishmael and Keturah (25:1-4, 12-16). Arabia’s population was thus drawn from several lines, all of them part of the one family that came from the ark.

wordNotes.explanation: The Hebrew form can be read as “court of death,” but the name corresponds to Hadramaut, the incense-producing kingdom of southern Arabia. The Hebrew spelling likely adapted a foreign name to familiar sounds, so the apparent meaning should not be pressed.

verses.bibleText: And Hadoram, and Uzal, and Diklah,

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Hadoram is probably an Arabian tribe; the same name belongs to an unrelated prince in David’s time (1 Chronicles 18:10). Uzal has long been identified with the old name of Sanaa, the highland capital of Yemen. Ezekiel lists traders “going to and fro” who brought “bright iron, cassia, and calamus” to Tyre, and the Hebrew there may be read “from Uzal” (Ezekiel 27:19).

Diklah means “palm grove,” a fitting name for a south Arabian oasis where date palms flourished. Each of these names reflects settled communities along the incense and spice routes of the Arabian peninsula.

wordNotes.explanation: Uzal is traditionally the ancient name of Sanaa in Yemen. If Ezekiel 27:19 refers to traders from Uzal, the city shipped iron goods and aromatic spices northward to the markets of Phoenicia, showing how Joktan’s descendants were tied into international commerce.

verses.bibleText: And Obal, and Abimael, and Sheba,

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Obal, written Ebal in 1 Chronicles 1:22, may belong to southwest Arabia, between the coast and the highlands of Yemen. Abimael is otherwise unknown, but his name, “my father is God,” contains the divine name El. Names like this suggest that the knowledge of the one God had not yet been lost among the peoples descended from Noah, even as idolatry spread.

Sheba appears here as a son of Joktan, though verse 7 named a Sheba among the descendants of Cush. The Sabaeans of southern Arabia may have drawn on both lines through intermarriage and settlement, or the name may describe two related groups. Job’s servants were attacked by raiding Sabeans (Job 1:15), and the Sabaean kingdom became famous for its trade in incense and gold.

wordNotes.explanation: The name combines “father,” a connecting element, and El, the common Semitic word for God. Theophoric names of this kind, such as Abiel and Eliab, express trust or belonging. Its presence in Joktan’s line hints at an inherited memory of the Creator among Arabia’s early peoples.

verses.bibleText: And Ophir, and Havilah, and Jobab: all these were the sons of Joktan.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Ophir became the most famous of Joktan’s descendants because of its gold. Solomon’s fleet, sailing from Ezion-geber on the Red Sea, brought back four hundred and twenty talents of gold from Ophir, along with almug wood and precious stones (1 Kings 9:26-28; 10:11). “Gold of Ophir” became a phrase for the finest gold (Job 28:16; Psalm 45:9). Its location is debated. Suggestions include southwest Arabia, the African coast opposite it, and even India. Since Joktan’s territory is bounded in Arabia (10:30), the people of Ophir most likely lived there, though their name may have attached to a wider trading region.

Havilah appears again, as in verse 7, perhaps a region of Arabia where Cushite and Joktanite peoples lived side by side. Genesis 2:11-12 had already associated a land called Havilah with fine gold before the flood. Jobab has not been identified. The summary “all these were the sons of Joktan” closes a list of thirteen names.

Isaiah takes up Ophir’s gold to make a point about human worth. In the day of the LORD’s judgment, he says, “I will make a man more precious than fine gold; even a man than the golden wedge of Ophir” (Isaiah 13:12). The price God paid for human beings exceeds all gold: believers were redeemed “not with corruptible things, as silver and gold … but with the precious blood of Christ” (1 Peter 1:18-19).

wordNotes.explanation: Ophir names both a descendant of Joktan and the land associated with him. An ostracon from Tell Qasile in Israel records “gold of Ophir for Beth-horon,” confirming that the name served as a recognized designation of high-quality gold in the Israelite period.

verses.bibleText: And their dwelling was from Mesha, as thou goest unto Sephar a mount of the east.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And their dwelling was from Mesha, as thou goest unto Sephar a mount of the east.” Like Canaan’s in verse 19, Joktan’s territory receives boundaries. Neither point can be fixed with certainty. Mesha may lie in northern or northwestern Arabia, while Sephar is often connected with Zafar or Dhofar on the southern coast, near which highlands rise from the sea. The description encloses a broad stretch of the Arabian peninsula.

“A mount of the east” may refer to the mountain country of southern Arabia. “The east” in Genesis is simply the region east of Canaan, home of “the people of the east” among whom Jacob found Laban (29:1) and from whose mountains Balaam came (Numbers 23:7). It was also the direction of Cain’s departure (4:16) and the starting point of Babel’s builders (11:2), but the phrase here is geographic.

After this verse Joktan’s family leaves the narrative of Genesis, much as Ishmael’s twelve princes are recorded and then set aside (25:12-18). Peoples outside the chosen line are named, located, and remembered by God. Isaiah later calls the inhabitants of the Arabian deserts to “sing unto the LORD a new song” and “give glory unto the LORD” (Isaiah 42:10-12), and Arabians were among those who heard the gospel at Pentecost (Acts 2:11).

wordNotes.term: הַר הַקֶּדֶם (har haqqedem) — a mount of the east
wordNotes.explanation: Qedem means “front” and, since the ancients oriented themselves facing sunrise, “east.” The phrase can describe the eastern hill country generally. Balaam uses a related expression for his homeland in Aram, showing that “the east” could cover a wide region beyond Canaan.

verses.bibleText: These are the sons of Shem, after their families, after their tongues, in their lands, after their nations.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“These are the sons of Shem, after their families, after their tongues, in their lands, after their nations.” Shem’s branch closes with the same refrain used for Japheth and Ham (10:5, 20). The chosen line receives no special formula. Shem’s descendants are divided by language and territory like everyone else, and they share in the scattering of Babel.

Shem’s line also includes nations that turned against God’s people. Assyria descended from Asshur, and Elam’s king joined the raid on the cities of the plain (14:1-12). Even Abraham’s own fathers “served other gods” beyond the river (Joshua 24:2). Being a Shemite did not make anyone faithful.

The New Testament presses this lesson. John the Baptist warned those who trusted in their ancestry, “think not to say within yourselves, We have Abraham to our father: for I say unto you, that God is able of these stones to raise up children unto Abraham” (Matthew 3:9). Paul concluded that “they which are of faith, the same are the children of Abraham” (Galatians 3:7). Membership in God’s family comes through faith in the promised Seed, and that faith is open to the descendants of all three sons of Noah.

wordNotes.explanation: Lashon means the tongue as a bodily organ and, by extension, a language. The refrains place language alongside kinship and land as a mark of each people. Zephaniah foresees God giving the peoples “a pure language,” literally a purified lip, so they may call on the LORD together.

verses.bibleText: These are the families of the sons of Noah, after their generations, in their nations: and by these were the nations divided in the earth after the flood.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“These are the families of the sons of Noah, after their generations, in their nations: and by these were the nations divided in the earth after the flood.” The closing verse returns to the language of verse 1 and frames the whole chapter. Every people named has been traced back to Shem, Ham, or Japheth, and every one of them to Noah.

The table contains seventy names, a number that combines seven and ten, both associated with completeness in Scripture. The list stands for the whole world of nations. The same number reappears when Jacob’s household goes down to Egypt as “threescore and ten” persons (46:27; Exodus 1:5), as if Israel were a small version of the family of nations, chosen to bless the rest. Moses may have this correspondence in view when he says that God “set the bounds of the people according to the number of the children of Israel” (Deuteronomy 32:8). When Jesus later sent out seventy messengers ahead of him (Luke 10:1), the number would have recalled this table to Jewish hearers.

The chapter teaches the unity of the human race. All nations descend from one family that came through the flood. No theory of separate origins and no claim of racial superiority can stand with this chapter or with Paul’s declaration that God “hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth” (Acts 17:26). All share the same need, for “all have sinned” (Romans 3:23), and the same Lord “is rich unto all that call upon him” (Romans 10:12).

“Divided … after the flood” leads directly into chapter 11, which explains how the division happened at Babel. Then chapter 12 begins God’s answer. He calls Abram and promises, “in thee shall all families of the earth be blessed” (12:3). Paul calls that promise the gospel preached beforehand (Galatians 3:8).

The story ends where it began, with every nation in view. Before Christ returns, the everlasting gospel is to be preached “unto every nation, and kindred, and tongue, and people” (Revelation 14:6; Matthew 24:14), and the redeemed will stand before the throne as a multitude from all of them (Revelation 7:9). The nations divided in Genesis 10 will be gathered at last around the Lamb.

wordNotes.term: נִפְרְדוּ הַגּוֹיִם (nifredu haggoyim) — were the nations divided
wordNotes.explanation: The verb parad means to separate or branch off; it describes the river of Eden parting into four heads and Abram and Lot separating from each other. Here it describes peoples spreading out from a common source into distinct nations, as verse 5 had said of the coastlands.

Mabbul is used almost exclusively of Noah’s flood, the worldwide judgment that ended the old world. Its repetition here shows that the nations of the table all date from the new beginning God gave after that event. The psalmist celebrates the LORD enthroned over the flood as King forever.

teachingNotes.openingQuestion: Why would God place a long list of ancient nations in Scripture right before he calls one man, Abram?
teachingNotes.mainPoint: Every nation descends from one family preserved through the flood, and the God who scattered the peoples is already preparing to bless them all through the chosen line of Shem.
discussionQuestions: What does the shared descent of all nations from Noah teach about racial pride and prejudice?
Why does Nimrod receive more attention than any other figure, and what kind of greatness does he represent?
How does the description of Canaan’s borders prepare for the promises God will give Abraham?
Why is Shem’s line placed last even though it is introduced first?
How do Pentecost and the vision of a great multitude from every nation answer the dividing of the earth?
commonMisunderstandings: Noah’s words about Canaan do not curse any skin color or justify slavery; the table makes every people a branch of one family.
The dividing of the earth in Peleg’s days refers to the scattering of peoples at Babel and is not a description of continents splitting apart.
The table is selective and does not claim to list every tribe on earth.
Nimrod’s fame “before the LORD” is not divine approval of his empire building.
teachingNotes.emphasis: Hold together the unity of humanity and the particular line of promise: God narrows his focus to Shem and Eber so that blessing may reach every family named in the table.
teachingNotes.closingAppeal: Receive every neighbor as kin from the one family God made, and trust the Seed of Abraham through whom the scattered nations are gathered again.

evangelisticNotes.mainDoctrinalTheme: God made all nations of one blood, judged human pride by scattering it, and in Christ gathers people from every nation into one family.
flow: Every person on earth traces back to one family that God preserved through the flood.
Human pride, pictured in Nimrod and Babel, sought greatness apart from God and brought division.
God chose the line of Shem and Eber to bring the promised Seed into the world.
In Christ the barriers between peoples fall, and the everlasting gospel goes to every nation, kindred, tongue, and people.
Each hearer is invited to join the gathered family of God before Christ returns.
simpleIllustrations: A family tree on a wall shows cousins who have never met; Genesis 10 shows the whole human race on one tree.
A map with many borders still sits on one globe; the nations are divided, but they share one Maker and one origin.
evangelisticNotes.appealQuestion: Will you accept your place in the family God is gathering from every nation through Jesus Christ?
cautions: Do not use the sons of Noah to assign moral rank or destiny to any modern ethnic group.
Do not claim certainty for identifications of ancient names that remain uncertain.
Do not make the table a tool for nationalism; its aim is the blessing of all families of the earth.

reflectionQuestions: Do I treat people of other nations and backgrounds as members of my own extended family?
Where am I tempted, like Nimrod, to measure success by influence, building, and a famous name?
How does knowing that God set the bounds of the nations shape my view of my own place and time?
What part can I take in carrying the gospel to peoples who seem distant from me?
Am I living as one who belongs to the line of promise by faith in Christ?
